name: italian green sauce and pesto
instructions:
A progression of italian pasta sauces built around green herbs and vegetables — read in REVERSE order compared to the tomato master. Where the tomato master starts simple and builds up to the raw pesto, the green master starts at the raw pesto (variant A, the canonical simple mortar version) and moves outward toward a more complex blended-and-cream-cooked sauce (variant B, my mother's Mike & Family recipe). Variant C (food processor) is NOT a basil pesto path — it's the greens-only fresh-pasta-salad direction. THE TOOL-LEAF MATRIX governs everything: EVERYTHING WORKS IN A MORTAR; the BLENDER works with BASIL ONLY; the FOOD PROCESSOR works with SPINACH/GREENS ONLY, not basil (see notes). For tomato-based italian sauces (Hazan's 3-ingredient, halfway-pesto, sicilian pesto rosso), see the tomato pasta sauce family — [[marcella-tomato-sauce]], [[sicilian-pesto-rosso]], [[vodka-sauce]], [[pasta-piperade]], [[marcella-eggplant-sauce]] (all tagged 'tomato pasta sauce').

=== VARIANT A — CLASSIC MORTAR PESTO (BARE-BONES) ===

The canonical simple form. Made in a mortar and pestle. Soft ingredients only — the mortar can't break down anything fibrous or hard. Everything valid in this recipe works in the mortar: basil builds and the non-basil greens builds alike.

INGREDIENTS:
- fresh basil (canonical); spinach or baby spring mix also work (mortar builds only — and lemon becomes NON-OPTIONAL with them, see notes)
- pine nuts (canonical); cashews + sunflower seeds TOGETHER simulate pine nut (works in all variants)
- garlic (raw, 1 clove — see notes on managing potency)
- olive oil (good quality)
- grated parmesan cheese
- black pepper
- salt to taste
- pasta

PROCEDURE:
1. In a mortar, pound garlic with a pinch of salt into a paste.
2. Add the greens and nuts. Pound to a rough paste — the goal is a coarse texture, not smooth.
3. Drizzle in olive oil while stirring with the pestle until you get a loose, oily paste.
4. Fold in grated parmesan and black pepper. Salt to taste.
5. Toss with cooked pasta. Optional finish (BASIL BUILDS ONLY): a small amount of heavy cream at the end for a richer read, and/or fresh chopped tomatoes for brightness. (If using both cream AND tomatoes as a finish, cook the tomato chunks in the cream FIRST before adding to the pesto — same step as variant B's technique, confirmed to work well as a variant A finish. See notes. Cream + the non-basil greens is an anti-pattern — see notes.)

=== VARIANT B — PENNE PASTA WITH PESTO (MIKE & FAMILY / MY MOTHER'S RECIPE) — BASIL ONLY ===

My mother's recipe, sourced from In Style magazine in 1994 and credited to 'Mike & Family.' A blender pesto folded into a reduced cream sauce with canned diced tomatoes. Definitively NOT a traditional pesto — this is a cream-based pasta sauce with pesto as the flavor component. BASIL ONLY — the blender does not take the non-basil greens (see the tool-leaf matrix).

INGREDIENTS:
- 2 cups fresh basil leaves MINIMUM (buy 3 sprigs at the store instead of 1-2 — see notes; go bigger)
- 1/4 cup pine nuts (or the cashew + sunflower seed simulation)
- 4 cloves garlic
- 1/2 tsp salt
- 1/8 tsp black pepper
- 1/2 cup olive oil
- 1/2 cup grated parmesan cheese, divided
- 1 1/2 cups heavy whipping cream
- 1 can DICED TOMATOES (my modification — replaces the original 'one large ripe tomato')
- 3/4 lb cooked penne pasta

PROCEDURE:
1. MAKE THE PESTO: place basil, pine nuts, garlic, salt, and pepper in a blender. Process until basil is finely chopped.
2. With the blade running, gradually add olive oil in a steady stream. Scrape down sides and process until well blended.
3. Transfer pesto to a small bowl. Stir in 1/4 cup of the parmesan. Set aside.
4. REDUCE THE CREAM WITH TOMATOES: in a saucepan over medium-high heat, combine the heavy cream and the canned diced tomatoes (drained lightly if very wet). Bring to a boil.
5. COOK THE TOMATOES IN THE CREAM BEFORE ADDING PESTO: reduce heat and simmer until the tomatoes have cooked into the cream (~5-8 min) and the sauce has thickened slightly. Don't skip this — see notes on why cooking the tomatoes in cream first is important.
6. FOLD IN THE PESTO AND REMAINING CHEESE: add the pesto and the remaining 1/4 cup parmesan. Cook 3-4 min until heated through.
7. Toss pasta with the sauce. Serve.

=== VARIANT C — FOOD PROCESSOR GREENS SAUCE — SPINACH/GREENS ONLY, NOT BASIL ===

The food processor path — for SPINACH and BABY SPRING MIX only, NOT basil (the food processor under-extracts basil's flavor; see the tool-leaf matrix). This is the fresh-pasta-salad direction of the family, not a pesto.

INGREDIENTS: spinach or baby spring mix, the nuts (pine nuts, or cashews + sunflower seeds together), garlic, parmesan, olive oil, LEMON (non-optional with these greens — see notes), salt, black pepper. NO CREAM (anti-pattern with the non-basil greens — see notes).

PROCEDURE:
1. Add the greens, nuts, peeled garlic, salt, and pepper to a food processor.
2. Pulse to a coarse chop. Add grated parmesan and a drizzle of olive oil to loosen; pulse again briefly.
3. Fold in more olive oil off the blades to reach the consistency you want. Lemon juice in — non-optional here.
4. Toss with cooked pasta.
notes:
THE PROGRESSION — CANONICAL RAW PESTO → CREAM-COOKED PESTO PASTA (REVERSE OF THE TOMATO FAMILY): the green sauce family runs in reverse of the tomato family. Traditional italian green cooking centers on the raw mortar pesto (variant A); traditional italian tomato cooking centers on the cooked sauce (variant A over there). So the ladder here starts at the canonical simple form and moves outward toward a cooked-cream-and-canned-tomato version (variant B, Mike & Family / my mother's recipe). Variant C is the sideways branch: the non-basil greens direction.

=== THE TOOL-LEAF MATRIX — WHO GOES IN WHAT ===

- MORTAR: EVERYTHING works in a mortar — basil builds and the spinach/spring-mix builds alike. Overall the mortar is better, for the greens just like for basil.
- BLENDER: BASIL ONLY. Never the non-basil greens — the blender turns them into goo and extracts the wrong thing.
- FOOD PROCESSOR: SPINACH/GREENS ONLY, never basil — it under-extracts basil's aromatic oils (the chopping action doesn't rupture the cells the way a mortar's crushing or a blender's shear does), so a food-processor basil pesto reads basil-flavored but not basil-forward.

WHY THE GREENS BREAK THE BLENDER RULE: the non-basil builds aren't about FLAVOR EXTRACTION — they're about making a FRESH PASTA SALAD. Coarse, fresh, bright. The blender's whole value is aggressive extraction, which is exactly the wrong thing for these leaves.

=== LEAVES — THE NON-TRADITIONAL AXIS ===

- BASIL: canonical; the pesto identity.
- SPINACH and BABY SPRING MIX: can work — but NEVER with a blender, and NEVER with cream. Mortar (or food processor) only. When using them, LEMON BECOMES NON-OPTIONAL — the greens builds need the acid to read bright pasta-salad rather than flat leaf paste.
- KALE and ARUGULA: make BAD pestos, ALWAYS. Clashing — no tool rescues them.
- PARSLEY: doesn't work in the mortar — too fibrous, doesn't break down by hand.

=== NUTS — THE NON-TRADITIONAL AXIS ===

- PINE NUTS: canonical.
- CASHEWS + SUNFLOWER SEEDS TOGETHER: simulate pine nut — in ALL variants, including the blender. The two together, not either alone, is the simulation.
- ALMONDS: CLASHING — not just a texture/blending problem (too hard for the mortar); they clash with the green flavor profiles. Almonds are for red pesto ([[sicilian-pesto-rosso]]).
- WALNUTS: CLASHING as well.

=== CREAM RULES ===

- CREAM + BASIL: valid. Variant B is built on it; variant A takes a SMALL amount of cream as an optional finish at the end.
- CREAM + THE NON-BASIL GREENS: ANTI-PATTERN. The spinach/spring-mix builds are fresh pasta salads — cream is the wrong direction for them. Lemon and olive oil carry those instead.

=== TOMATO — CHOPPED WHOLE TOMATO IS GOOD IN ALL VARIANTS ===

Chopped whole (fresh) tomato is a good addition across the board. If using cream with basil, COOK THE TOMATO CHUNKS IN THE CREAM FIRST (per variant B's reduction step — confirmed to work well as a variant A finish too): the tomato loses its raw-tart edge and integrates with the cream before hitting the pesto, so the finished dish reads cohesive rather than as pesto-with-raw-tomato-on-top. For the mortar, fresh only — finely chopped and rinsed; canned tomatoes are the wrong texture for a mortar dish (canned diced is variant B's territory).

=== VARIANT A NOTES ===

PESTLE RULES — SOFT THINGS ONLY: the mortar can't break down fibrous or hard ingredients. Soft leaves (basil, spinach, baby spring mix) and soft nuts (pine nuts, cashews, sunflower seeds) pestle well; parsley and hard nuts don't.

GARLIC IN PESTLE PESTO IS POTENT: raw garlic pounded into a paste is much more aggressive than raw garlic in a blender-smoothed sauce. Two ways to manage:
- Use sparingly — one clove per batch is usually enough.
- Pre-macerate the garlic in lemon juice for a few minutes, then drain aggressively before pestling. Softens the raw garlic bite; the trap is leaving too much juice and making the pesto too lemony.

CREAM IS OPTIONAL AS A FINISH — SMALL AMOUNTS, BASIL BUILDS ONLY: a small amount of heavy cream stirred in at the end works as a richer finish on the basil pesto. Not traditional but fine — it's the bridge into variant B territory. Never on the greens builds (see CREAM RULES).

=== VARIANT B NOTES — MY MOTHER'S RECIPE (MIKE & FAMILY) ===

SOURCE: In Style magazine, 1994. Credited to 'Mike & Family.' My mother's recipe. It always comes out well when I make it, which is why it lives here as the default variant B despite some steps that give me pause.

BUY MORE BASIL THAN THE RECIPE SUGGESTS — 2 CUPS IS THE MINIMUM: the recipe says 2 cups fresh basil leaves. Treat that as the floor, not the target. Buy 3 sprigs at the grocery store instead of 1-2; the sauce reads more basil-forward and the pesto more distinctly pesto with the extra. If you buy the recipe amount you'll be shy on basil.

TOMATO — CANNED DICED, NOT ONE LARGE FRESH TOMATO (MY MODIFICATION): the original calls for 'one large ripe juicy tomato.' I substitute a can of diced tomatoes.

COOKING THE TOMATOES IN CREAM BEFORE THE PESTO GOES IN — LOAD-BEARING STEP: bring the cream and the diced tomatoes to a boil together, then simmer 5-8 min BEFORE adding the pesto. The tomatoes need cooking in the cream first — otherwise they're too tart, and the finished sauce reads sharp/acidic rather than integrated. Skip the cooking step and the sauce has an off, uncooked-tomato edge; do it right and the tomatoes become part of the cream base rather than sitting on top of it.

=== VARIANT B — STEPS THAT GIVE ME PAUSE (BUT IT WORKS) ===

CAUTION 1 — CREAM ISN'T BLENDED WITH THE PESTO: the recipe processes the basil in olive oil (traditional pesto liquid), then folds the pesto into a separately-cooked cream. It doesn't take advantage of putting cream in the blender with the basil, which would let the sauce blend tighter (cream provides emulsion body a lot better than olive oil does for a pesto). This is a real missed opportunity in the technique. Something worth trying: some or all of the cream in the blender with the basil, then fold the resulting cream-pesto into the reduced tomato-cream. Untested; the recipe as written works, so I've never rocked the boat.

CAUTION 2 — HEATING THE BASIL: the pesto (basil + pine nuts + garlic + oil + cheese) gets folded into a hot cream-and-tomato reduction and cooked 3-4 min. This violates the standard basil-goes-off-heat rule (see italian stuffed peppers, master pesto pasta, etc). Traditional pesto handling says basil loses its aromatic character on heat and turns muddy/dark. Somehow this recipe survives that — the basil stays green enough and the sauce reads bright rather than muddy. My hypothesis on why:
- The cream buffers the heat and keeps the basil from oxidizing as fast as it would in an oil-only sauce.
- The pesto-in-oil step (before the cream) coats the basil in olive oil first, which may protect the leaves through the brief cream cook.
- Ultra-blended basil is more bitter than mortar-pounded basil (aggressive cell breakdown releases more bitter compounds), and briefly cooking it might mellow that bitterness — a hidden feature of the technique.
Still cautious about this. It works consistently in practice; I don't fully understand why.

CAUTION 3 — CONCENTRATED FLAVOR VIA HEATED-CREAM REDUCTION: another possible reason the recipe works: heating and reducing the cream might concentrate the sauce's flavor in a way that a raw cream splash can't. Cold cream added to pasta at the end is a diluent — it disperses flavor. A cream that's been reduced with tomatoes carries more concentrated tomato-and-dairy character before the pesto goes in. That concentration might be part of what lets the basil-on-heat step work without the sauce reading watery or muddy. Combined with the buffering hypothesis above, the cream is doing multiple structural jobs at once — dilution buffer + concentration medium + flavor-mixing solvent.

=== VARIANT C NOTES — THE GREENS PASTA-SALAD DIRECTION ===

NOT A PESTO SUBSTITUTE: variant C is its own thing — spinach or baby spring mix, coarse-chopped in the food processor, lemon-forward, no cream. Reach for it when you want the fresh-pasta-salad read; reach for A or B when you want pesto. Don't put basil through the food processor expecting pesto — it under-extracts (see the tool-leaf matrix).

FOOD-PROCESSOR MECHANICS (why it suits the greens): the processor doesn't NEED oil to run — the blades chop without liquid, so oil stays a texture finish added off the blades (impossible to over-oil, unlike the blender). Nuts stay coarse rather than crushing into paste. Both properties serve the coarse/fresh pasta-salad goal.

=== SHARED / CROSS-VARIANT NOTES ===

STORE-BOUGHT BASIL PESTO IS CLASHING EVERYWHERE: jarred pesto isn't good enough for any variant. The pestle has texture and freshness a jar can't match; the blender-and-cream variant has technique specificity a jar wasn't built for. Don't substitute.

BASIL IS THE PESTO IDENTITY: variants A (basil build) and B are pestos, and basil is structural in them — without it the dish stops reading as pesto. The spinach/spring-mix builds (mortar or variant C) are deliberately NOT pestos — they're the fresh-pasta-salad branch of the family, with lemon doing the lifting.

SHORT PASTA IN ALL VARIANTS: this family prefers short pasta shapes. Long strands don't grip the sauce. Penne is the workhorse (and specifically what variant B calls for).
